To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) visual categorization is fast, (b) it can be done at the superordinate but not at the basic level, and (c) the first 120 msec of visual categorization are not sufficient for basic level categorizations.
(1) visual categorization can be performed in less than 150 msec, (2) visual categorization is hierarchical, and (3) visual categorization requires additional analysis of the visual information.

the saccade latencies to the target images were surprisingly stable (around 155 msec), and accuracy dropped from 80% to chance levels when the categorization level was changed from superordinate to basic.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether and when the brain can recognize an object as a dog, a cat, or an animal.
the speed of visual categorization at different levels.
the question of what information is available in the visual system during the first 100 msec of processing.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the visual system has a fast and efficient access to coarse object representations that provide information about object identity at the superordinate (animals) but not at the basic level.

there is no advantage in processing basic level information in comparison to superordinate level information, but that the basic level information is not yet fully available within the first 120 msec of visual object categorisation.
categorization is a hierarchical process, but the speed of processing is not.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
visual categorization is a hierarchical process that starts with the identification of a superordinate level and then proceeds toward a more specific categorization.
visual object categorization can be fast and efficient at the superordinate levels, but the basic level requires additional visual analysis.
the visual system can access coarse visual representations that allow recognition at the superordinate category, but more detailed analysis is needed to allow recognition at the basic category.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the speed–accuracy trade-off is a fundamental property of visual object recognition.
the visual system can access the superordinate level very early in visual processing, but it needs additional visual analysis to access basic level representations.
visual object recognition is a hierarchical process, but the hierarchy is not necessarily a strict one.
